newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian economists tip mark peg up to 1,400 lev.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian economists tip mark peg up to 1,400 lev.

text.p: The Economy Institute of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences on Monday proposed pegging the lev to the German mark as anchor currency in a currency board arrangement at a rate between 1,300 and 1,400.

"Overvaluing the lev when fixing the rate to the anchor currency is one of the subtle ways to undermine the successful implementation of the currency board," the institute's director, Ivan Angelov, told a news conference.
"Our estimates show that at the time of introduction the rate should be between 1,300 and 1,400 to the mark."
An overvalued lev would hinder production and exports and stimulate imports, resulting in a high trade deficit and slower economic growth, he said.

Under a $657 million agreement with the International Monetary Fund, Bulgaria has pledged to introduce in July a restrictive monetary mechanism, known as a currency board, designed to restore confidence in its shaky banks and currency.
The system requires the amount of levs in circulation to be matched by the amount of foreign exchange reserves and bans central bank lending to the govenment and commercial banks.

Earlier on Monday Finance Minister Muravei Radev said it was possible to announce the anchor currency and the rate at which the lev will be fixed later this week, to prevent excessive speculation on the domestic currency market. He did not elaborate.
Under preliminary plans parliament was expected to announce the currency and the rate a week before the launch of the currency board system.
Radev said recently that the exchange rate assumed in the draft 1997 budget frame was 1,600 levs per dollar and 1,000 to the mark.
The mark traded on Monday at around 920 levs per dollar.

Bulgaria has yet to finalise this year's budget, transform the central bank to accommodate the currency board, appoint a new central bank board and revise the Banking Act before launching the currency board system.
The institute warned of possible new banking failures after the introduction of the currency board.
"A new wave of bank failures is possible after the introduction of a currency board because the central bank will be banned from lending," one of the institute's experts, Ivanka Kraininska, said.

Most Bulgarian banks have so far relied on central bank re-financing and their survival in the first months of the currency board's operation, when the economy and domestic markets will still be relatively stagnant, is questionable, said Kraininska.

Under a revision of the Banking Bill, which has yet to be finalised by parliament this month, the central bank can seek insolvency of a commercial bank if it proves to be illiquid for longer than seven days.
In the past year the central bank has placed in receivership and sought bankruptcy through the courts for 16 local banks -- one third of the total.
Angelov said the currency board, if successfuly implemented, would gradually boost lending to the economy as interest rates stabilise. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
